blessing upon us . as we assemble on this occasion of the 130th Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of Masons of California a nd Hawaii.
We pray Thou wilt pour forth Thy grace and favor upon our beloved and
highl y es teemed Grand Master. the Most Worshipful D o nald G. Ingalls.

leadership and broad-visioned inspiration of our Grand Master, enabling
us to reach greater levels of moral growth and organizational achi e vement.

Need I say what an exciting and meaningful event this will be for our
Hawaiian Brethren and for us all?
I have travelled outside our Grand Jurisdiction twice this year. The first
time was in early February to Baja California at the invitation of the Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of Baja California , Juan Manuel Beltran
Perez. In Tijuana and Tecate we met with other Brothers in the First International Convention of the Three Californias. (Baja being considered
as North and South).
The event coincided with the celebration of the anniversary of the Mexican Constitution and a mutual torch of Brothe rhood and patriotism was
lit that may well have a future influence on many facets of American as well
as Fraternal interchange with our good neighbors to the South.
It is hoped that this conference may become an annual event and I sincerely urge such a consideration by our incoming Grand Master.
My other trip outside the Jurisdiction was to attend the Annual Conference of the Grand Masters of North America held this year in Colorado
Springs. Your Grand Master was highly honored by being invited to be
the keynote speaker at the opening session which was attended not only
by the Grand Masters, Deputy Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries of
North America, but also by Grand Masters from European jurisdictions
and other Masonic leaders. I was also honored by being appointed Chairman of the Committee to Plan the Celebration Program in honor of the
250th Anniversary of the birth of George Washington. The program will
be presented in Washington. D.C. in 1982.
This annuar meeting of the Masonic leaders of this great continent is
always a rewarding experience and the interchange of ideas and programs
affecting Freemasonry, its leadership, needs and challenges is most worthwhile.
Another most unexpected honor came to your Grand Master during this
conference when the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge National of
France, Most Worshipful A. L Derosiere, appointed him an honorary Past
Grand Senior Warden of the Grand Lodge National of France, the highest
honor that body can confer upon a non-French Mason.
Another very special event I attended was held on March 8 in Oakland
when the Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems. P.Jst Grand Master and
Grand Secretary for so many years, received his 50-year Golden Veterans
Award before a sell-out crowd of family, friends and Brethren.
How does one judge the value of such a man and Mason? By the number
of years of service? By the quality of that service? I only know that by
whatever criteria Brother Ed is judged, the final conclusion will be the
same-his value to Freemasonry, his community and his family. was, and
is, inestimable.

There arc other Grand Jurisdictions in th e United States and elsewhere
that havl: recently severed their fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge
of Belgium. They have based their action on an alleged decision on the
part of the Grand Lodge of Belgium to suppress the obligation for a belief
in Clod as a condition of admission as well as certain alleged statements
to support this suppression on the part of the Grand Master. Herman Buskcns.
Before acting in this matter. your Grand Master requested written evidence to support the charges and a state ment from the Grand Lodge of
Belgium clarifying its position.
On reviewing the collected data. it appears that the Grand Master
named served only one month in office before resigning and that the
Grand Secretary. Pierre Clerbois has been serving as acting Grand Master
since that time. We have been assured in writing by Brother Clcrbois that
the Grand Lodge of Belgium has in no way modified the basic principles
according to which it was created and that it works to the glory of the
Great Architecc of che Universe.
Quoted is Article I of its Constitution: "Freemasonry affirms the existence of God. the Supreme Being. described under the name of the Great
Architect of che Universe. All adepts arc required to admit this affirmation. This requirement is absolute and cannot give rise to any compromise
or restriction ...
Broth er Clcrbois answers a second complaint of permitting non-recognized Masons to visit in his grand jurisdiction by stating such visits "have
always bee n forbidden and still are and this has regularly been reminded
by Grand Committee to all Worshipful Masters . .,
Until such time as solid evidence to the contrary is presented, r chose
to accept the word of a Brother Mason and took no action in this matter.

Numher I : Committee to Study Organizatio nal Structure of Grand Lodge
In a special repo rt to the Grand Master in September of 1978, the Committee on Policy and Ge neral Purposes recommende d that the incoming
Gra nd Master appoi nt a hlue-ribbon commissio n to care full y examine the
organization al stru cture of the Grand Lodge of California, and also that
of other Grand Jur isdictions. and to formally repo rt the results of its study
a nd its conclusions at the 1979 Annual Communica tion. I duly appointed
such a commission.
In discussing the matter of deadline with the Deputy Gra nd Master, it
was agreed tha t in the time remaining it wo uld be impossible for the Commission to conclude its study this yea r. I therefore recommend th at the
Commision be continued and instructed to make its report at the 1980
Annual Communica tion.
For you r info rm ation, the areas to be considered include the service
provided members by the Grand Lodge and m ay be divided into three
categories: (1) Operatio n- the administrati on o f the services and functio ns of the G rand Lod ge, (2) Program-th e activities of the Grand Lodge
in the areas of Masonic ed ucatio n , leaders hip improvemen t, inspiration.
etc., (3) Rit ua l- the preservation and teaching of the California Masonic
ritual to insure confor mity and q uality of the work.

In recent years there have been informal proposals suggesting a clear
se paration of the ritual function from the o ther functions of Grand Lodge .
It has been suggested that a weakness of o ur present structure is that Inspectors are respon sible to two separately elected primary officers of the
Grand Lodge: Grand Master and Grand Lecturer. While their duties are
quite different. it is suggested that some overlap of functi on (due in part
to the convenience of th e Division and District organization) occurs and
has caused possible conflict of authority and loyalty. In addition to this area.
the Commission is to broadly interpret its purpose to be to examine. study,
compare and report conclusions on all three areas: operation . prog ram
a nd ritual.

Number 2: Grand Master's Seminars
Your Grand Master s incerely believes these programs, one held in each
Division during the year. create an open door of understanding and cooperation betwee n th e constituent Lodges a nd their Grand Lodge . Besides
se rving as a refresher course to all in attendance as to what Grand Lodge
trul y is, its purposes. services and functions, it also serves as an informal
a nd friendly forum where the Grand Maste r, many of the Grand Lodge
officers and Committeemen. may sit down with Lodge Maste rs. Wardens
a nd Officers to openly discuss mutual proble ms and concerns.
It is in essence ta king the Grand Lodge, too often thought of as a sepa rate and elite group situated here in San Francisco. out into the field. out
to you Brethren who truly co nstitute the Grand Lodge ·of California. It
provides you with the opport unity to exchange ideas and comment with
th e Grand Master who m you ha ve elected to se rve you .
I firmly believe th at the Grand Master's Seminar program is a viable
process of mutual ed uca tio n and frat e rnal interchange, and that it assures
the Officers of all the constituent Lodges a n additional opportun ity during
the year to make certain their Lodge is rece iving the services and educational aspects of Grand Lodge it deserves a nd is entitled to .
I therefore recommend to the incoming Grand Master th a t t he G rand
Maste r's Seminar program be continued, in whatever working forma t he
may deem prope r. during the ensuing Grand Lodge year.

From out of the vastness of the Pacific Ocean once came a people to the
most isolated archipelago in the world - these Hawaiian Islands.
Those early Polynesians were a proud race. claiming the great gods as
a ncestors, and the y imprinted their royal character upon all the Hawaiia n
tom orrows that would follow.
Their unique cultural contrihution still expresses itself in modern Hawaii. inextricably woven into the loom of time itself. Freemasonry. that
ancient and honorable Brotherhood of men dedicated to self-improvement
and the hetterment of all men, recognizes this influence. for part of Freemasonry's strength and beauty is its acceptance of such contributions as
a necessary step toward the ultimate Brotherhood of all men.
The ceremony you arc about to witness is based upon certain ancient
customs whose significance is explained in the ritual itself. Portions of the
original ceremonies were adopted by the Masonic fraternity and the one
now used is identical to the one used by George Washington as acting
G rand Master of Maryland when he layed the cornerstone of the Capitol
Building in Washington D.C.
Masonry first came to these Islands in 1778 in the person of Captain
James Cook. a member of the Grand Lodge of England. but Masonry
officially became part of the Hawaiian lore in 1843 when "Lodge le
Progres de J'Oceane .. was given the power to confer degrees under a dispensation of the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite of France . and this
•
Lodge tirst met on board the barque "Ajax" in Honolulu harbor.
When Masonry was established in California in 1850. the opportunity
for connection with a geographically closer. English-speaking Grand
Lodge. led Hawaiian Masons to petition for a charter. and thus commenced what would eventually become a long and fruitful relationship.
The tirst laying of a cornerstone with Masonic honors in Hawaii was in
1860. when His Majesty Kamehameha IV. a past master of Lodge le
Progres. acting as Grnnd Master for the occasion. officiated in laying the
foundation stone for the Queens Hospital in Honolulu.
His Majesty Kamehameha V was present in 1872 when the cornerstone
of the Judiciary Building was laid with Masonic ritual.
In 1879, the cornerstone was laid for the tirst Masonic Hall in Honolulu
at the corner of Fort and Queen Streets. His Majesty. David Kalaka ua .
was present. wearing his Past Master's jewel. accompanied by Queen Kapio lani and the he ir apparent Liliuokalani.
Also in 1879. the cornerstone was laid for lolani Palace on December
31. the hirthday of Queen Kapiolani. The date was selected by the King
himse lf as a signiticant one to exemplify th e role of Masonry in the Islands.
Both the King and the Governor. John 0. Dominis. wore the insignia of
the thirt y-t hird degree of Masonry at the event. which was attended by
represe ntatives from foreign powers and local government officials. Many
attractive and colorfully attired ladies assemhled under and around the:
spacious tent erected on the grounds for the occasion.
As Masonry grew in Hawaii. so did the numher of cornerstone layings.
including; the Masonic llall on Alakea Street in Honolulu in 1892: the

PROCEEDINGS OF rH E

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN I A

Masonic Hall in Kahului . Maui in 1906; the Masonic 1lall in Hilo in 1909;
thl· Honolulu Librarv in 1911 ; the 1lonolulu Scottish Rite Cathedral in
1922. where the wo~king too ls used by Governor Farrington. acti ng as
Grand Master. were the same solid silver ones donated by King Kalakaua
in 1879. Other cornerstone layings include the Territorial Office Building
in 1925. the auditorium of the McKinley High School in 1927. and the City
and County Building in 1928. all in Ho nolulu . The cornerstone for Scholicld Lodge No. -U.1 on Oahu was laid in 1968.
In considering this history. it becomes apparent that the Masonic Cornerstone Ceremony is truly a shining thread in that beaut iful patte rn of
life called H awaii .
At one time the foundation stone. or cornerstone. of a building was one
truly squared and perfected in all respects so that the edifice which would
rise from it would be both beautiful and strong.
Modern methods of co nstruction have rendered this technique unnecessary. but the sy mbology of building man 's c haracter from a true and
perfect base has remained unchanged. and is the true mea ning of th e modern ritual.
Freemasonry has a strong concern that it publicly display its support of
the institutions of fn:edom. That is why FrecmiJsons lay cornerstones. and
it is with great pride that the l\1asons of the sove reign State of Hawaii now
proceed with this ceremony.

PROCLAMATION

PROCLAMATION
MASONI C HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH - MAY, 1979
TO:

All Masonic Lodges in California and Hawaii

Dear Brethren:
When the great artist Holman Hunt's painting "The Light of the World"
was unveiled, a critic complained that the representation of Christ standing in a garden at midnight, holding a lantern and knocking on a door,
was in error.
"Look", the critic pointed out to the artist, "There is no
handle on the doo r." "That is correct", the artist replied, "That door
represents the doorway to the human heart.
It c an o nly be opened from
inside 11 •
And so it is also with the hearts of California and Hawaii Masons who
are again called upon to open their hearts "from i nside" so that with
dignity and happiness, the members of our Masonic family at Union City and
Co v ina may be secure in the warmth of our Masonic Homes. This opportunity
for every Mason to participate unselfishly in a true act of Brotherly Love
is one of the brightest jewels worn in the crown of our honorable and
ancient Fraternity.
St. Matthew said, "A good man out of the good measure of the heart
bringeth forth good things ••• " In the Old Testament it is asked, "Lord,
who shall sojourn in Thy Tabernacle? Who shall dwell upon Thy Holy hill?"
And it is answered, "He that walks uprightly, and works righteousness, and
speaks the truth in his heart . "
Now, my Brethren, is the time for every Mason to gladly open his
heart in gratitude for blessings received , to work uprightly as a true
Brother, knowing the righteousness of his kindly act is the expression of
the truth in his heart.
With faith in that willingness of the heart, I proclaim the month of
May, 1979, to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
and direct this Proclamation to be read at Stated Meetings held during the
months of April and May, 1979 .
I furthe r direct that e ach LOdge send a
copy of this Proclamation to each of its members or reproduce i t in its
Trestleboard .
Don't wait for the month of May to act -- truly, every month is
Masonic Homes Endowment Month!

Dear Brethren:
"All that is necessary for evil to triwnph, is
f or good men to do nothing."
- Edmund Burke
Men of Masoni c character were among the majority of those who, in 1776,
thrust the flame of freedom above the clawing grasp of tyranny and their
voices cry out to us today across the bridge of more than two hundred years
t o " hold high that flame!" That flame still burns, my Brethren, and its
source is still t he Constitution of the United States of America .
The dream of liberty, which began in the hearts of men who knew firsthand what t yranny was, i s ours now if we can keep it. Our enemies from
without , the within, arrogant, and in connivance with self-serving and determined segments o f society who see anarchy as a release from individual
r esponsibi l it y , believe they can wrest that dream from us. They constantly
seek to weaken and final ly destroy the source of our freedom.
We Masons believe that to surrender our constitutio nal rights is not the
way of the American people .
It is not the essence of the national characte r
which won us independence, t he West, two World wars and the he arts and minds
of millions upon millions of people a c ross the fac e of this planet. Masons
have always been, and shall continue to be, guardians of what this sacred
docwnent stands for and fu lly realize that the freedom i t has assured us is
indeed an ephemei;al f lame unless tended with constancy, devotion and patriotic
understanding.
Masons and men of Masonic character have always been among the watchmen
o n the walls of freedom. We know full wel l that "Except the Lord keep the
Cit y, the watc hmen waketh but in vain. " As Masons alert and ready to act,
under God, with faith, vision , courage and willing hearts, daring to do the
right -- we shall not fail our responsibi lity. In that spirit, I proclaim
the Month of September t o be
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
and direct this Proclamation to be read at the August and September, 1979
Stated Meetings.

by
Donald G. Ingalls
Grand Master, California
"Oh. Lord. give us fearless men!
Men to meet the trials of life .
With faith. vision. steadfast
hearts and willing hands.
Men who dare to do the right! ..
My Brethren: at this very minute. this gentle hrotherho od we call Freemasonry is forbidden to exist or is under attack in the majority of the
nations of this world. Freemason s. men like you and me. still undergo
persecutio n. torture . and imprisonm ent and arc la helled as outlaws to a
large majority of the population of this earth.
What is our "crime?" What is it that we Freemason s stand for that is
an anathema to certain societies of men? The answer is germane to a
proper considerat ion of the theme of this I 979 Conferenc e of Grand Masters in North America:
" FRELMAsO NRY-

01.n AND NEW FRoNTll: Rs··

The answer is that Freemason s arc persecuted for the "crime" of heing
tolerant. universal . emhracing all men and religions : opposing intoleranc e.
bigotry. spiritual despotism . and political tyranny: and for our dedication
to hringing about a brotherho od of man under the fatherhood of God .
The old Masonic frontiers lie be hind us . at rest in hloody honor. omitted
or half-hidde n in the intricate pattern of history's tapestry. Only those line
golden threads. woven indestructi vely into the loom of time b y men who
were Masons. shine forth todav to remind the thoughtful scholar that indeed. in those days. were thc;c giants in the earth! and they called one
another Brother'
From outside our Craft there is. from time to time. recognitio n of Freemasonry's role in history. sometimes from unexpecte d sources .
During the Bicentenn ial year of these United States of America. the
popular French Magazine PARIS MATCH in its 1976 May issue featured
an article on American Democracy. and pointed out that in great measure
it was the fervent desire for freedom hy Freemason s on both sides of the
Atlantic that led to the success of the revolution . The article noted that
the concepts expressed in the new constitutio n reflected in great part the
hasic ideals which we know were tirst enumerate d in Anderson \ Masonic
Constituti on of 1723. It stated further that the virtues which ennohle man
are taught and cultivated in Masonic Temples. and that it was men of this
ennobled character who surrounde d General George Washingto n. himself

53

a Freemason . as generals and advisors . Brother George Washingto n
wrote . "The virtues taught in Masonry arc makers of perfection in private
life. and set rule~ for the mo~t elevated duties of the state ."
Those dedicated and stalwart men . many of them Freemason s . came to
the frontiers of this great land with a dream of lihcrty in their hearts.
knowing lirsthand what tyranny was, and passed on to us their dreams in
written form: the Constituti on of the United States.
Men of Masonic character were among the majority of those who in
1776 thrust the flame of freedom a hove the grasp of tyranny, and their
voices cry out acros!. two hundred years to all free men today to .. hold
high that tlamc . ··
We arc honor-hou nd to heed that cry. my Brethren. for today we stand
at a new fro ntier . and before us looms the unexplore d and dangerous wilderness of the future. Portentiou s rumblings of storms ahead mav be heard
on every hand and. as at the old frontiers . it is once again the rmperative
ohligation of Freemason s everywher e to ~ird their loins for the battle of
survival. to diligently pursue their goals of brotherho od and individual liherty at whatever the personal cost: to thrill awake to the dangers which
confront them . and ahove all , lo realize that the prize is wo rth the gamefor we are talking of the survival of Freemason ry and of freedom itself.
Thank God for those carlv-dav Masons whose dedication to their Masonic principles made demo~racy and freedom realities. The 4uestion is:
If democracy , if freedom. depend now on the Masons here in this room
today-wil l they continue?
"'The virtues taught in Masonry arc makers of perfection in private life.
and set rules for the most elevated duties of the state."" Brother George
Washingto n saicJ .
Was he talking about politics'.' I think not. my Brethren: not as we think
of politics in this day. He meant a code of conduct which leads good men
to become better men . men who through the expression of their thoughts
and the example of their actions help make a better world for hctter men.
and wiser men for a wiser world.
It is proper that politics per se. is held to have no place in the structure
of our Craft when asse mhlc.:d in Grand or Constitute nt Lodges. Neither
bo<ly is or should he a forum to arousl' contention or confusion among our
brothers .
But freedom and survival is not a mere political considerat ion. it is a
hasic right of mankind~
Freedom is the very essence of the character of the United States of
America. and of all fn.:e nations evervwher e . Indeed. the character of free
nations and Freemaso nry is irrevocahl y intermingl ed and the threat to one
is at the same time a threat to the other: for where there is nn frel•dom.
my Brethren. there is no Freemason ry; and where th e re is no Freemasonry. there is no freedom .
The perpetuati on of freedom. then . is not only of proper Masonic concern. hut Masonic survival itself depends upon it 1
Our enemies. those who would destroy freedom and Freemason ry. have
already crossed the new frontiers. They wait in ambuscad es along the rug-

(', RAN D L ODGE O F CALI F OR~IA

ged trails ahead. These enemies. some outside the circled wagons of freedom: some within o ur own camps. arrogant and in connivance with selfserving. determined segments of our society who see anarchy as a release
from individual responsibility. work to undermine and erode our fortiAcations of freedom with an ever-increasing flood of coercion. violence, trickery and deceit-and they arc clever. and they never sleep.
President .lames Madison was correct whe n he said. "There are more
instunces of the abridge ment of th e freedom of the people by gradual and
silent encroachments of those in power. than by violent usurputions."
The modus operandi of our e nemies inside our camp may be analogized
by describing an old biological experiment: if a frog is dropped into boiling
water. he'll leap out a nd save himself. But if you place him in a pan of
cool water and then heat the wate r grndually. the frog is lulled into a sense
of security and goes to sleep--just prior to being parboiled ~
To submit to tyranny. to give a way our freedoms under the guise of
progressively broad constitutional interpretations, by buying the old
sucker-pitch that you can get something for nothing. by hoping that everything will come out all right just as long as we get ours-is no t the way
of a free people. It is not the essence of the national character which won
America independence. conquered the old frontiers. won us two world
wars. and earned us the respect of billions of men and women around the
face of this earth'
Our enemies outside the circled wagons of freedom are less subtle, and
their attack is direct. But before considering them. le t us try to d efi ne thi s
rare and precious thing we call "freedom ...
We know certainly that it is an ephemeral flame unless tended with constancy, devotion and understanding. Its light has flickered and gone out
many times in the history of man. We know that to those of us living in
free countries it is a way of life. while to others less fortunate. it is an
enigma. a dream. or a non-reality that they ca nnot even understand.
By way of illustra tion. former Secretary of the Treasury of the United
States William E. Simon tells of a meeting held in Moscow in 1975 between American and Russian officials ...
On the surface. things went well. detente remained intact and peace was
maintained. But under the smooth facade of Mr. Brezhnev and the other
Russians. Mr. Simon sensed a deep emotional difference . some profound
way in which the Russians were not like the Americans.
The Americans knew that outside their rooms. which were tilled with
sturgeon. caviar. and vodka-induced joviality. in some o ther dimension of
reality, there was a n immense. oppressed populace.
Somewhere , outside their walls, people were ill-clad. ill-housed. ill-fed
and un-free. Some at that very moment were being torn from their homes
and famili es and hurled into jails and insane asylums for the "crime" of
disagreeing with these same jovial hosts.
Later, when the Americans departed and th eir plane taxied to the runway of the airport outside Moscow. all fell silent. Then. the plane lifted
off and they heard the thump-thump of the landing gear locking up, and

they reali zed that they were no longer on Soviet soil. Spontaneously.
everyone o n the plane b urst into applause!
It was like they we re staging a great escape!
It was the sudd e n vanishing of all th e me nac ing th ings that characte rize
the Sovie t Union. the intrusion you can feel but cannot see-t he unspoken
awareness of unseen oppression.
Thi: Americans we re flying home-to freedom!
At that moment of liftoff, Mr. Simon wa s able to put into words t hat
se nse of deep, unnam e able difference betwee n the Soviet officials a nd the
Americans: it was the difference between men who have never kn own
freedom-and men who were horn free .
Freedo m: a state of liberty as opposed to contincment-se lf-determini:!tion in th o ught anJ choice-liberty of movement and speech-powe r

THE FINANCES OF T H E CRAFT IN GENERAL

The minimum initiation fee of $50.00 for me mbership in a Masonic
Lodge in California has remained unchanged for more than 35 years.
The average initiation fee for all California Lo dges was $98. 26 last year
with yearly dues ranging from a low of$ I 2.00 to a high of $66.00.
Sometimes overlooked in the disposition of the individual Lodge ·s
funds. is the need for adequate reserves to provide for the unknown and
unscheduled demands for relief of distressed Brethren and their families .
Section 2900 of th e California Masonic Code clearly establishes the responsibility of the indi vidual Lodge concerning relief:
" A Lo dge must relieve its own members. the ir widows and
o rphans . It shall sec to it according to its circumstanc es and
ability. that the needy Brethren of its ow n membership arc not
suffered to want o r to be made a burden to o thers.··

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFO RNIA

fiJ

Many Lodges meet this responsibilit y adequately and well. Unfortunately. there arc man y constituent Lodges in this Jurisdiction that do not.
o r cannot. provide for the proper relief of their membe rs and/or their widows. It is respectfully suggested that each Lodge examine the adequacy
of their fund s to meet the req uirements of Section 2900.
To the end that all of o ur Lodges be financially able to render adequate
relief and establish proper reserves. I therefore recommend that the Finance Committee of this Grand Lodge review the present minimum initiation fee of our constituent Lodges and give consideratio n to establishing
a percentage of the initiatio n fee as a Lodge endowment for membe rs·
relief and also make such recommenda tions as they may deem proper for
consideratio n at the 1980 Annual Communica tion.

As provided by law. minutes of meetings. financial records. vouchers.
supporting papers and books for the Masonic Homes of California. the
California Masonic Memorial Temple. the California Masonic Retirement
Plan. the Masonic Hornes Endowment Board and the California Masonic

program.
Because our Fraternity , like business. is not immune to gove rnmental
encroachments. evergrowing technical requirements. restrictions. reports
and analyses continue to be imposed upon us in the various areas of our
Masonic activities by different governmental agencies. We are fortunate
to have. within the membership of the Fraternity . technical expertise on
which we may call to develop adequate responses for these ever increasing
requirements and to maintain in all areas a position of non-dependence
upon any governmental subsidies.

tary Edward H . Siems pointed out in his annual report the necessity for,
and propriety of, an active dues committee in each Constituent Lodge. He
re-emphasiz ed the need for comprehens ive reports by these committees
to the Lodges prior to the suspension action on delinquent members.
While it is recognized that there is no alternative other than suspension
for some delinquent members. caution should be exercised by the dues
committee so that their recommenda tions to the Lodges are based upon
thorough investigation of the members' circumstanc es.
However , awareness of the downward trend , rather than fearful concern
over membership totals , should be our attitude. Elsewhere, during this
Communica tion. you will hear reports by your Grand Lodge Officers and
Committeem en which reflect the over-all rejuvenation of our Masonic activities and continuation of our Fraternity as a vital , active influence in our
local communitie s.

PERSO NNF.I.

Because of retirements and natural attrition several new employees
have been added to our staff during the last year. We recognize that personnel changes in any business or organization arc inevitable and. though
replacement s are not always easy to find, the total number of our employees remains unchanged . We are proud of the fact. and the Fraternity
should feel fortunate to have an office staffed with competent . qualified
employees eager to perform in a professional manner the duties assigned
to them.
MEMB ERSHIP

Summary figures for the last year show a continuation of a trend in
membership which started in I 966. In that year we recorded the first net
loss in total membership since 1941 . A peak total of 244 ,586 members was
reco rded in the summary figures of June 30, 1965 and as of June 30. 1979,
the total was 202,027. This reflects a net loss of 42.559 members or 17.4% .
While quantity will never replace quality. we should he aware , not only
in Grand Lodge but in the constituent Lodges as well . of the continuation
of this net decline. Also , we should be aware of the increase in the consolidation of Lodges which has been occurring, particularly in the metropolitan areas. From a high of 71 l Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction in
1968 there is currently a total of 651 Lodges in California and Hawaii-a
loss of 60 Lodges or 8.4% .
The greatest single factor causing the net decline in membership is
death. During the last five years there has been a loss of 28,036 members
for that reason. However, we in the office are encouraged as the monthly
membership reports submitted by the Lodges reflect the fact that throughout the Jurisdiction many new and younger members are becoming Master
Masons.
A more disturbing factor is the continuation of the large number of suspensions for non-paymen t of dues. During the last five years there has
been lost to the total membership 7.763 members. In 1964 Grand Seere-

A CCOUNTING RECORDS

We reported last year that studies were continuing toward the feasibility
of extending data processing techniques in the membership and accounting
areas. Since that time a highly reputable firm was engaged to conduct a
thorough , non-biased and professional analysis of our office procedures
and record keeping. They were chosen only after careful study and interviews held with comparable organization s doing similar work. Following
favorable responses from your Elective Grand Lodge Officers, the Chairman of the Finance Committee, and members of the Fiscal Advisory Committee to our proposal, the analytical study was contracted by your Grand
Secretary .
After a job by job analysis and detailed review of the work flow in the
office, a complete report was made reflecting those areas of our ope rations
which could be advantaged by appropriate data processing equipment.
Bearing in mind that any new rec.ord keeping equipment considered
should fit our functions rather than our functions fitting the equipment ,
requests for proposals were sent to ten vendor companies. Proposals have
been received from seven . Following review of the proposals by your
Grand Secretary. members of the Fiscal Advisory Committee , our Chief
Accountant , the Executive Director of the Masonic Homes and other concerned Masons, the system best suited to our needs is under current review
and is recommend ed for installation as soon as practicable.
PARAPHERN ALIA

A complete set of new Grand Lodge Officers' aprons are being worn
for the first time at this Annual Communica tion. This allows for the old
Grand Lodge set to be placed in service in the field as the "Northern Traveling Set". The "Northern Traveling Set" presently in use has become
quite shoddy and is being retired from use . It is anticipated that another
set of aprons will be required in the near future to replace the current

At the 1977 Al'lnual Communication. the Trial Review Committee reported as fo l lows:
"The trial transcript in this case. including the accused 's own statements. contains uncnntroverted evidence that. although he could have
done so. the accused failed to make an effective attempt to prevent o r to
d iscourage th e furnishings of three pornographic film<, to a sixtee n year
old member of the Order o f DcMolay for the pu rpose of showing them
to other minor young men . The evidence shows th a t the accused was a
DeMolay advi sor wh o knew o f th e plan to furnis h such pornographic tilms
to the DeMolav and of the DeMolav's intention to show them to o ther
min o r young men . By his own tcstim,ony the accused claimed that o ne of
the accused"s e mployees wa-; to furnish ~uch tilms. It is uncontroverted
also that the accused knowingl y facil ita ted the furnishing of such films hy
his employee and the picking up of the films at the accused's home by th e
DeMolay for the purpose of showing them to his football team . The accused 's explanations fall short of excusing him in any way for his acts a nd
his failure to act .
The tindings of act hy the commissioners on the two precise specitications were on conflicting evidence . One spceitication charged the accused
with actually furnishing the films anti a pro,iector and the other specification charged the accused with providing his home on anothe r ot·casio n

I

PROCEEDINGS OF T HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for a stag party at which pornographic films were shown to DeMolays and
at which liquor was served to DeMolays. While the Trail Review Committee cannot set aside the findings of the commissioners that the accused
was not guilty of the precise specifications set forth in the original charge.
it is clear from the evidence that the accused failed in his duties as a Mason
and is guilty of un-Masonic conduct."
The Grand Lodge then adopted the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that this Grand Lodge affirm the findings hy the commissioners on the original charge; but that this Grand Lodge direct the
Junior Warden of Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469 to charge the accused with
a violation of Masonic law by reason of his failure to make any effective
attempt to prevent the furnishing of pornographic films to a sixteen year
old member of the Order of DeMolay for the purpose of showing them
to other minor young men and by reason of his knowingly facilitating the
furnishing of such films for such purpose, and that the trial on such charge
or charges be in a Lodge to be designated hy the Grand Master.
Action was taken in accordance with the Resolution. The new trial transcript reflects that the Trial Master convened the trial. The Commissione rs
were excused during which time the Trial Commissioner heard oral arguments (having received written arguments) that the First Specitication
failed to constitute a Masonic Charge and that the Second Specification
constituted double jeopardy. The Trail Master ruled that the First Specification failed to specifically allege the accused had knowledge of the furnishing of the pornographic film and on that basis was defective. With
respect to the Second Specification. the Trial Commissioner ruled that
double jeopardy existed and therefore was defective.
The Trial Review Committee agrees with the holding on the First Specification. It appears clear, however. that properly drafted. the First Specification will indeed constitute a serious Masonic offense.
The Trial Review Committee has concluded that the double jeopa rdy
holding on the Second Specification is in error both as to Mason ic Law
and California Law. Further. the Committee notes the debate on the 1977
Resolution by the Grand Lodge focused almost solely on the issue of double jeopardy and the Grand Lodge after hearing the doubl e jeopardy arg uments voted in favor of th e Resolution directing new charges to be filed.
Your Committeee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOL YEO (1), that this Grand Lodge affirm the ruling of the Trial
Commissioner that the First Specification failed to state a chargeable offense because it did not specifically allege the accused had any knowledge
of the furnishing of the pornographie film; (2). that this Grand Lodge reverse the ruling of the Trial Commissioner in that th e Second Specification
does not constitute double jeopardy under Maso nic Law or California
Law ; (3). that this Grand Lodge direct a Trial Maste r to be appointed by
the Grand Master to conduct the trial of the accused:
(a) On the F irst Specification to be ame nd ed by the Junior Warden
of Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469 to state a Masonic offense. and
(b) O n the Second Specification in its current form.

This proceeding was initiated against a member of Confidence Lodge
No. 203. F. & A. M .. for reducing secret work to writing.
Jn 1978. the matter was returned hy Grand Lodge to Confidence Lodge
No. 203 for proper proceedings. with direction that the Junior Warden
charge the accused with violation of C.M.C. Section 3306 (f), that a Trial
Master be appointed and the matter properly tried.
The accused entered an amended written plea dated April 3, 1979 of
"Nola Contre" (sic.) or "no contest". On November 30. 1977. the accused
wrote the following: "'You presented me with charges of Unmasonic Conduct-' reducing secret work to writing'. I admit that the papers involved
arc in my handwriting and that I am guilty of the offense charged. This
writing was done as an aid to my memory personally. and should have
heen destroyed immediately after it had served its temporar y purpose."
The Trial Master found the accused not guilty of violation of C.M.C.
Section 3306 ( f) on the basis that the actual writing of the secret work was
not in evidence and the November 30. 1977 letter was written when the
accused was in "extreme duress" and in a '"state of depression."
The Committee on Trial Review believes that the lack of physical evidence of the writing is insufficient to justify a finding of "Not Guilty" in
light of the accused's written admissions of violation of C.M.C. Section
3306 (f) and the proferred excuse for the violation of his obligation is unacceptable.
Your Committee therefore submits the following resolution:
RESOL YEO. that the finding of not guilty made by the Trial Master
he reversed a11d the penalty fixed at expulsion.

This proceeding was initiated against a member of Monrovia Lodge No.
308. F. & A. M .. for misappropriatio n of DeMolay funds.
The accused admitted the charge of un-Masonic Cond uct a nd the Trial
Master made a finding of guilty a nd fixed the penalty at reprimand in open
Lodge.
While the accused was under seve re personal financial pressures at the
time. by his own written stateme nt. he acknowledged that he " took what
at th e time was the easiest way ." It is notable that the accused was serving
as an Advisor to t he DeMolay and h ad in his cha rge not only the funds
of the organization. but the responsibility for setting an exe mpla ry example for the youth .
The offense constituted a violation of California criminal law involving
moral turpitude as well as cheating. wrongin g and defrauding a Masonic
Lodge, through the DeMolay Chapter under its sponsorship.
The offense is such a basic. serious a nd knowing violation of moral law.
particularly for one in a position of responsibility for a DeMolay Chapter.
that the Committee on Trial Review recommends that the penalty be increased from reprimand in open Lodge to expulsion.

affirmed and the pe nalty b e tixed at expulsion.

R E HABILIFA TION
The progress of the reh abi litation of our reside ntial building and the
construction of the new Charles Sedam Ce nte r is proceedi ng slowly but
surely . Workm e n a nd equipment arri ve daily to provide ma ny opportunities for "sidewa lk superintending ."
All residents li ving in the main building a rc e njoying the improvements
that provide private bathrooms and the addit ional security of new fire preventi ve devices .
While the middle section of the reside ntial huilding is he ing remodeleu
everyone has had to learn new pathways and directions to reach a reas
within the facility. All of the administrative offices a re in temporary lo cations and access between the No rth and South wings is o nly available
at th e ground fl oo r level.
Alth ough the inconveniences make it diffic ult for residen ts , employees
and visito rs. a spirit of adventure a nd cooperation permea tes the daily

again hosted the members of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board for

of men attended the opening of Grand Lodge and a large numher of residents attended the Monday night entertainment. and on Thursday the
installation of Officers. Also. several of our residents assisted with the
Home's exhibit and supplied information to those who attended the Annual Communication. Another nice tradition was continued with our Masonic Home art show in September. Close to a hundred items displaying
the talents of our residents were entered in the various categories (in. eluding oil painting. photography. stitchery and ceramics). The judges
award went to Mrs. Trudie Leslie for her original stitchery.
The oldest tradition associated with the Home (as rememhered hy residents and staff) took place on the third Saturday in August. The 66th
"Jam and Jelly Day" was attended by the Officers and some committee
memhers of the East Bay Past Matrons Association. plus Grand Chapter
ofticers and our Grand Master. A display of their handwork items and a
check for the purchase of jams, jellies and juices. represented their yearlong efforts toward the care and comfort of our residents.
We celebrated some very important milestones in the lives of our family.
Ten of the couples have been married fifty or more years. The 66th an niversary was reached hy Brother and Mrs Burton Cartwright (Granada

ceremony that does not occur every year. On April 5. residents Estelle
Robinson and Arthur Mahry were joined in marriage at the Home hy our
Chaplain. Reverend Phillip Johnson.
Our Grand Master. Most Worshipful Donald Ingalls and his lady were
honored on May 2nd. at dinner and a reception. By their attendance. the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes and several Grand Lodge Officers. afforded 20 ladies of the Home an opportunity to escort their gentlemen

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
The Publication Board of Grand Lodge consists of the Grand Master,
the Grand Secretary, such advisors as deemed desirable, and an Editorin-Chief appointed by the Grand Master . It is responsible for the publication and distributio n of the California Freemason.
The magazine is completing its 26th year o f publication and during this
period nearly 17 million copies have been issued .. During the pas.t year
840.000 copies were mailed to members of California L~dges. to patd su?scribers. and to Masonic jurisdictions both in the Umted States and in
foreign countries.
.
. . .
.
/\s the official publication of the Grand Lodge its objective 1s to bnng
forth the best repo rts on the progress of Freemasonry in California to the
officers of the constituent Lodges. to those who regularly attend Lodge
meetings. and especially to those who do not participate in Lodge activities
as actively as in the past.
The last four quarterly editions of the magazine have been ~lied with
reports of Public Schools and Constitution observances, Masomc Homes
activities. scholarship presentations hy the California Masonic Foundation. cornerstone ceremonies. and literally hundreds of photographs and
stories of Lavman's Nights, Golden Veterans and Hiram Awards. Articles
have covered a wide range of Masonically related subjects. historic and
current.
The California Freemason is mat.le readable and provocative o nly
through the continuing interest of the officers of the Lodges and their m:mhers. who make it so bv their contributions. During the past year the edito r
has heen able, to the best of his knowledge. to print every su bmitted
Lodge event story. Only by so doing will the California Freemason continue to tell the story of what is really happening to Masonry through o ut
the State of California.
Respectfully submitted.

growth in our state that are not convenient to e xisting Lodges and Jo have

Committee on Chaners can not instigate the procedures. but we stand
ready to assist and advise any interested Brethren . A manual is a vaila b le
that detai ls a ll the steps in forming a Lodge.

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE

There is n o need to emphasize that the rapid increase in the rate o f
inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index is o ne of the great problems fac ing the natio n. For the past fiftee n years ( 1964-1978) dividends ,
interest and capital appreciation of stocks. bonds and gove rnment secu rities have just abou t equa lled the ave rage annual infla tion ra te increase of
5.4% . However. in the last five years ( 1973-1978), inflation has increased
at a rate of 8% a nd the inc rease in 1978 ove r 1977 was 9% . Now we a re
e ntering a period o f double digit inflation. All of this points o ~t the need
for the highest pe rfo rman ce from the invest me nt of funds, working toward
the highest rate o f re turn , protecting capita l investment. a nd by t he most
knowledgeable ma nagement of fu nds achieving the total gain necessary
to help meet the monetary requirements of th e future.
T he Investme nt Committee is aware tha t changing marke t conditio ns,
money supply. intere st rates. intlat ionary pressures and othe r factors exert
continuing influe nce o n the secu rities marke t and call fo r the constant supervision of invested funds. Accordingly, the l nvestme n t Comm ittee is
utilizing the services of t wo monitoring firms to evaluate the performance
of the Gra nd Lodge portfolio and compare the results with funds of similar
size an d objectives.
T he California Masonic Code under section 1292 req uires that at least
twe nty percent of the fu nd s for investment of Grand Lo dge be in cash ~r
bank accounts. in obligations of the United States a nd the State of C alifornia . a nd in securities legal for sa vi ngs banks. T here is however, no definition of savings banks in the laws of California. T here has been presented
to this Grand Lodge a n emergent resolution to correct t his ambiguity. A
simila r resolutio n has been presented to improve the definition of investme nt funds o f the co nstitue nt Lodges. The Investment Committee recommends thei'r adoptio n .
It shall be the continuing policy of the Investment Committee to work
toward the conservation o f the invested funds a nd the highest income co mmensurate with sound in vestment practices.

The talented author, Robert Louis Stevenson, suffered from consumption the last years of his life. His sleepless nights were interrupted by
coughing and hacking. One morning Stevenson's wife entered his room
afte r a particularly difficult night and found the sunlight entering the room.
filtering through the many medicine bottles which lined the window sill.
"And J suppose you are going to tell me what a bright and cheery day it
is outside,'' she said. Stevenson replied, "You don't think Jam going to
allow a few medicine bottles to obscure my ho rizons do you?"
Brethren, like Stevenson, let's not allow our horizons to become obscured.
In a rece nt speech to the Nation, our President admonished us that our
country is experiencing a crisis of spi rit and confidence. It is a time of
disrespect for government. th e news medi a and o ld institutions. These are
symptoms- warning signs along the pathway of human existence that we
are traveling ; a time when two-thirds of our citizens do not take the time
to exercise their franchise and vote. The two greatest concerns of many
of o ur people today are how to find a place to park and what to do with
our garbage.
We are at a turning point in the history of our Country, and our Fraternity . One path leads to sure defeat and obscurity and th e other to certain
success and prosperity. We see m to have found all the answers. but the
important one-how to live with God. with others and with ourselves.
Freemasonry portrays the truth about man: it teaches the eternal truth
that despite all the differe nces that exist in race, color. traditio n. la nguage
and culture all men in the deepest sense are brothers.

way with a willingness of the heart. " Your presence here at this Annual
Communicatio n demonstrates the willingness in your hea rt and now it is
time to let the light of Masonry shine for a ll to see. There are thousands
of dedicated Freemasons who Jive and practice every day the tenets of our
Fraternity. They are living examples of Freemasonry in action and represe nt our present and future strength and hope.

jewel of his office. resolve to leave his Lodge at the conclusion of his tenure just a little stronger, just a little mo re active and prosperous than th e

Plan programs for the members and their wives which will be interesting-programs which are meaningful and useful-social activities which
are truly enjoyable. Remember, today 's world is a competitive world and
your Lodge is competing with television and a myriad of other activities
for your members' time. Be competitive-you will gain his attention and
make of him a more active member.

Public Schools Month and Constitution Observance Program
These are two traditional programs encouraged by our Grand Lodge
and observed by most constituent Lodges. Our support o f the public
school system will take on a new dimension this coming year as we are
faced with the proposed Family Choice Initiative-a new sounding name
which still means " the voucher system". Here is an opportunity to acquaint your membership with the meaning of this proposed legislation and
its effect on public education if such becomes Jaw.
Our Co nstitution Observance programs which focus attention on our
heritage as Americans and move us toward a dramatic red iscovery or remembering of the underlying reasons which led to the revolutionary birth
of American freedoms, all too frequently fall upon the same ears which
are present at most Lodge activities. I feel a strong effort should be made
by constituent Lodges as well as the Grand Lodge to make this observance
felt in the community by Mason and non-Mason alike.

Condition of Our Temples
Remember that non-Masons know and judge us by our actions as individual Masons and also hy our Temples. Strive to keep ou r Temples in
good repair, clean and inviting. I know we cannot all afford costly building
programs. particularly in this period of runaway inflation . but even the most
modest Temple will create a far better impression if maintained clean and
in good repair.

Ritual
By my lack of reference to o ur ritual work up to this point. please do
not feel that I am suggesting any less emphasis on our ritualistic endeavors.
The valuable lessons portrayed in our ritual represent the heart and soul
of our Fraternity. and I do not countenance any reduction in its impor-

GFNLRAL COMMENTS

Concern was expressed this past year that we as Masons and also as
indi viduals do not and cannot condone some of the things that are being
done in our local schools, and that we must he careful not to let the general
public be of the opinion that we support all the actions and programs of
our school districts. What we do support is the concept of PUBLIC EDUCATION. The 191-\0 Puhlic Schools Posters and other materials say
.. SUPPORT PUBLIC EDUCATION .. to help bring this important point
into focus.
Concern is still felt by the Public Schools Committee that too many
Lodges. particularly in the metropolitan areas. consider that they ha ve
accomplished their Masonic duty and responsibility by participating in a
large joint effort with other Lodges and/or Districts in a Public Schools
ObscrvarH.:c. The Committee congratulates these Lodges in their joint efforts and certainly encourages their continuance, but wishes to remind
each Lodge that there are numerous April and year-round projects for
individual Lodge participation. The Committee encourages each Lodge to
have a "project of their own.·· Many ideas and suggestions are contained
in the Lodge Manual. The Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools is
ready a nd willing to be of any assistance desired hy the Lodges and Masters.

The Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolutio n No. 20. carried over from the 1978 Annual Commun ication.
proposes to change the form of Applicat ion for Degrees or Affiliatio n so
that the applicant is giving his consent to the investiga tion of his characte r.
general reputatio n and mode of living. including criminal. financial and
health records.
Our 1977 revision on this su bject has been found deficient by eminent
legal counsel. and it should be changed to comply with the present State
and Federal Laws. Adoptio n of this Resolutio n will bring about that
needed complian ce.

"YES" vote.

(1978 Resolution No. 23)

The Committ ee 011 Jurisprudence:
The proponen ts of this Resolutio n seek to amend the Californi a Masonic Code to permit the use of a cipher or code ritual and to require the
Grand Lodge of Californi a to cause to be issued and published a cipher
ritual applying to all of the degrees. including floor and rod work: or to
approve the use of an existing cipher or code ritual equally extensive .

Brethren. the Ritual Committee recommended the form for delivery
now in use after many hours of study and consultation with me mbers of
the Clergy an d Funeral Directors . It has been in use_ now for ov~r three
vears and has received manv accolades. We of the R itual Committee recognize th at there are many. individual funeral officiants who ca n give the
service from various locations. hut there are many. many more who feel
more comfo rtable using the lectern only. and are just as well qualified
ritualistically as the foregoing.
The Ritual Committee has recommended the present service for all officiants in order that the delivery be uniform state-wide and not varying
from person to person and from locale to locale.
Options may be well intended. but with the officiant having complete
charge to m ake changes here and there to fit specific locales. our Funeral
Service would soon lose its dignity and impressiveness.
The outstanding success of our Maso nic Funeral Service over the last
three years has proven that this modification was desirable and necessary.
We therefore recommend a "NO"" vote.

WHEREAS. Section 1212 of the Masonic Code states that the duty of

WHEREAS. the geograrhic area of California and Hawaii is so vast

to accomplish this purpose: and
.
WHEREAS. there are 644 Lodges in this Jurisdiction. many of which
are in such remote areas that they are. for all practical purposes. out of
reach of Public Schools Committeemen. and in those areas that are presentlv reached by Committeemen. the disproportionate number of Lodges
to each Committeeman in many cases can result in merely superficial

WHEREAS. the task is further compounded because there are 7,471
public schools in California. as compared to only thirty Committeemen at
present. and the school hoards and administrato.rs of ma~y schools do not
seem to know that Masons actively support public education. nor arc they
<1ware th<1t Public Schools Week was originated by the Grand Master of
Masons in California. and continues to he observed. supported and sponsored annually hy the Craft; and
WHEREAS. new vistas ha,·e been opened to us in the media ...
television. radio and newsparers ... to the extent that warrants the
assigning of one Committeeman to that field on a yea_r-round _basis; and
WHEREAS. the burgeoning Volunteer Programs 111 practically every
Public School District in California , of which there arc l ,043. justify the
assignment of one Committeeman as a permanent liaison het~e~n th..:
Lodges and the schools for the purpose of obtaining greater part1c1pat1on
in these programs by memhers of the Craft: am.I
WHEREAS. all of the foregoing and much . much more can he accomplished with a few additional Committee members. for which the Co~­
mittee does not anticipate an increase in the budgeted exrcnse mer this
year .
. NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that the portion of Section
1202 of the California Masoni<.: Code which reads." ... on Puhlic Schools.
to consist of not less than fifteen nor more than thirty members" be
amended to read. " ... on Public Schools. to consist of not less than
fifteen nor more than forty memhers."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Uniform Code of By-Laws of Lodges, set forth in Section 2086.
makes provision for the name and number of a Lodge in Article I. Section
1, as follows:
"This Lodge shall be known by the name of
Lodge
No.
of Free and Accepted Masons; ... "
Article Xlll. Section 1. of The Uniform Code of By-Laws, outlines the
procedure for amendment of the Bv-Laws "so far as relates to the times
of meeting. and the amounts of fees. dues and disbursements bv the
Charity Committee.··
·
Based upon these Sections. we make these observations:
1. The name and number of a Lodge can be changed only by Grand
Lodge. Section 2022 C. M. C.
2. To seek a change of name (or number), a Lodge must effect an
amendment of its By-Laws. While Article XIII. Section 1. of The Uniform
Code of By-Laws of Lodges, concerning amendments, does not specifically mention change of name or number. we think that in a matter as
important as a name change the procedures set forth in this Article should
be followed. This requires the introduction of a Resolution in the Lodge
to ask Grand Lodge to approve the change of name in Article I. Section
1, of the Lodge's By-Laws at one Stated Meeting and then notice being
sent to the members of the Lodge of the proposed a mendment. and.
thereafter, having it voted on at the next Stated Meeting and approved by
a two-thirds vote. Following this. the Secretary shall note upon the minutes
of the Lodge the notice of proposed amendment when made. and when
transmitting the amendment to Grand Lodge for approval shall forward
a certificate. under seal, showing that the law has been complied with and
that the amendment has received the requisite vote.
3. No such amendment of the By-Laws of the Lodge shall be deemed
valid until approved by Grand Lodge. though they may be acted under
until the next Annual Communication if so authorized by the Grand
Master. Section 2082 C. M . C.
It is our conclusion that if the above procedure has been followed by
Patriot Lodge No. 737 then Resolution No. 11 is sufficient to carrv out
the intent of the Lodge. On the other hand. if the proper procedure has
not been followed then this Resolution is out of order.
The Grand Secretary has confirmed to us that the above procedure was
followed properly by Patriot Lodge No. 737. Consequently. in the opinion
of your Committee on Jurisprudence. Resolution No. 11 is sufficent to
carry out the intent of the Lodge.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge we move the adoption of this
Resolution.

Since Hillsborough Lodge No. 737 was originally chartered as such in
1954 and retained that name and number for a period of over twenty (20)
years until its consolidation with Milbrae Lodge No. 792 in January of
1975. and since the membership. now representative of both Lodges,
approved this recommended name change at a regular Stated Meeting on
4 May 1979, we recommend a "YES .. vote on this Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 11 proposes to change the name of Patriot Lodge No.
737 F. & A. M. to Hillsborough Lodge No. 737 F. & A. M. as it was
known to the community prior to its consolidation with Millbrae Lodge
No. 792 F. & A. M.

The Commiuee on By-Laws:
The Committee o n Bv-Laws concurred with the recommendation of the
Committee on Policy a~d General Purposes.

The Commiuee on Charters:
The Committee on Charters concurred with the recommendation of the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

PUBLIC FUND RAISING PROJECTSGRAND MASTER 'S APPROVAL
(12)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. Section 2070 of the California Masonic Code specifically
forbids the solicitation of the general public by any means whatsoever for
the purpose of raising funds to support the Lodge or Temple Associations;
and
WHEREAS. due to inflation and constantly rising costs of maintenance
and operations of Masonic Temples. it is becoming increasingly difficult
for sm all Lodges to continue without the imposing of a substantial dues
increase on its members; and
WHEREAS. it is the consensus of opinion of the undersigned sponsors
of this Resolution that a dues raise would only result in a loss of membership and would not be of any substantial value to these smaller Lodges;
and
WHEREAS. if the smaller Lodges are to remain in a healthy financial
condition and be able to retain their Temple buildings, they must find
some means of increasing income other than that of raising dues.
NOW, THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2070 be
amended to allow Lodges or Temple Associations that are either now or
may be in the future in financial distress to apply to the Grand Master for
permission to hold public fund raising projects or ventures and grant him
this authority.
Respectfully submitted.
DOUGLAS L. THOMAS. PM

The Committee on Temple Properties:
The Committee on Temple Properties is constantly dealing with the
problems of Lodges in financial distress. Accordingly. we appreciate the
objectives which this Resolution attempts to achieve .
We feel that Sections 2062 (C.M.C.) concerning solicitation and 2070
(C.M.C.) concerning commercial ventures both give the Grand Master
the power to approve the form and extent of solicitation and undertaking
of commercial ventures.
We note that many Temple Associations rent out Lodge facilities to
non-Masonic bodies which means that by implication and custom we
presently have some commercial intercourse with non-Masons.
While we feel that the formulation of guidelines as to what commercial
activities are presently allowable. or might be allowed by the Grand
Master may be desirable. we cannot agree with the provisions in Resolution No. 12 which provide for different treatment of constituent Lodges
based on financial condition .
Accordingly. the Committee on Temple Properties must respectfully
recommend a "NO" vote on Resolution No. 12.

this Grand Lodge while retaining his membership in such other Jurisdiction .

RESEARCH LODGES-MEM BERSHIP ELIGIBILITY
(13)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. a special classification of Constituent Lodges kno wn as
Research Lodges is provided for in Section 2124 of the California Masonic
Code; and
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 2124-2 now provides:
"Membership shall be limited to Master Masons in good standing in a
Lodge in this Jurisdiction. and shall cease if a member loses such status.
Membership may also be voluntarily severed at any time by resignation."; and
WHEREAS. manv California Master Masons are members of Research
Lodges in other jurisdictions which do not restrict membership only to
Master Masons of their jurisdiction. Most of these California Maste r
Masons are residents of California: and
WHEREAS. California Research Lodges receive many requests from
Master Masons of other jurisdictions for membership in our Research
Lodges. These Master Masons most often are not residents of California;
and
WHEREAS. it is desirable that Master Masons in good standing from
Grand Jurisdictions recognized by the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of California be permitted to be members of California Research
Lodges. Such membership should not permit them to vote or hold office
in California Research Lodges. There should not be a requirement of
residence in California.

251

Wherever reference is made in this Section to a Lodge of another Grand
Lodge. such reference means a Lodge of another Grand Lodge recognized by this Grand Lodge ...
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the California Masonic Code
Section 2124-2 be amended to read as follows:

"Membersh~p shall be limited to Master Masons in good standing. and
shall cease 1f a member loses such status. Membership may also be
voluntanly.severed at any time by resignation. Only Master Masons in
good standing in a Lodge in this Jurisdiction shall hold office and vote ."
Respectfully submitted.

Similar resolutions were presented in 1977 as Resolution No. 18 and in

remit dues of members who are unable to pay them. None of the circumc;tances cited in Resolution No . 15 should permit a Lodge to suspend a

me mber under any of these circumstances . The Lodge should remit his

As our Code presently reads. the criteria for eligibility to receive this

adopt this Resolution would seriously dilute the high esteem in which the

Mason for long and faithful service is completely defeated.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence. to which this Resolution has been
referred, reports as follows:
In view of increased interest rates on Time Certificates now being
offered by Bank and Savings Institutions. the proponent of Resolution
No. 19 seeks to amend Section 2804 of the California Ma sonic Code to
reduce the minimum amount to be charged for a life membership from
$250 to $150.
To carry out the intent of the proponent. your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED. that the 3rd sentence in the sixth line of Section 2804 of
the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"It must provide that life membership shall be granted upon payment
of a sum of money named therein , which sum shall in case the annual

The Committee 011 Polin a11d General Purposes:
Resolution No. 19 proposes that life membership in Lodges under this
Jurisdiction he established at a minimum of $150.00 per twelve dollars of
annual dues. except that Lodges may charge over this minimum provided
it is so indicated in the By-Laws of their respective Lodge.
The interest generated from Life Membership Funds. due to the small
percentage of members involved. is not sufficient to contribute any great
am o unt to ward current operating expenses of most Lodges. Operating
expense funds must come from the annual dues of the members. Also.
interest on Life Membership Funds invested in term certificates is not
always readily available to satisfy immediate requirements.
It is not anticipated that life memberships will increase in any great
numbers. particularly with many Lodges increasing their annual dues.
thereby raising life membership fees proportionately. Relocation of many
persons because of employment. schooling. etc .. which. in turn. has increased affiliations with other Lodges and diminished interest in life membership.
Further. in the past five years approximately 50 Lodges have consolidated. This could also be considered a deterrent to the purchase of a life
membership in that the future of some Lodges may be questionable in
the minds of its members.
Your CommitJee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "NO ..
vote on this Resolution.
Not Adopted.

WHEREAS. it is more desirable to have separate minutes of the special
meeting for the purpose of the funeral. rather than just a notation in the
minutes of the next Stated Meeting that the funeral had been conducted.

of Sectio n 290H remain as is to cover those situations where necessary,
but the language of the last sentence of Section 2908 be c hanged to read :
.. If, because of the absence of the Master o r one of the Wardens. the
Lodge may be opened for the purpose of the funeral service only by a
Past Master of said Lodge": and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the remaining portion of the last
sentence be incorporated in a new sentence reading: "If no member of
the Lodge is present who can recite the funeral service. the service may
be read by a qualified me mber": and

NOTE 5 - PRIOR PERIOD ADJUSTMENT
Effective July 1, 1978, Masonic Home s changed its basis of
accounting from the cash basis to the accrual basis in order to
conform with generally accepted accounting principles. At the same
time, the Homes changed its method of accounting for investments from
historical cost to fair market value.
The 1976 financial statements have been restated to give effect
to the change in accounting principles. TI1eir cumulative effect on
the Fund balances at June 30, 1977, follow:

Memorial Temple, a nonprofit corporation, at June 30, 1979 and 1978,

other auditing procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances,
ln our opinion, the aforementioned financial statements
present fairl' the financial position of California Masonic Foundation
at June 30, 1979 and 1978 and results of its operations and changes in
fund ba lanc e s f or the ye ar s then ended , in confo rmity with gener a lly
acc ep ted ac counting pr inc iples a pplied on a c ons i s tent ba s i s a f t e r
